title: Methane Blast at Sikkim Hydropower Tunnel Kills 20, Five Workers Still Missing
excerpt: A suspected methane gas explosion inside an under-construction tunnel at the NHPC's Teesta Stage-VI project in Namchi district trapped 25 workers on Monday. Rescue teams have recovered 20 bodies, with five workers still unaccounted for.
body:
• A methane gas explosion inside an under-construction tunnel at the NHPC Teesta Stage-VI Hydroelectric Project in Sikkim killed at least 20 workers, with five still missing as of late Tuesday night.
  • The blast on Monday afternoon trapped 25 workers about 1.5 km inside the tunnel; rescue teams using oxygen gear can only enter for 40 minutes at a time due to toxic methane concentrations.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced ex-gratia payments of ₹2 lakh per deceased worker from the PMNRF, while Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang ordered a high-level enquiry.
  • The tragedy renews scrutiny of safety standards in India's ambitious hydropower expansion, two years after the Teesta basin was devastated by a glacial lake outburst flood.

A suspected methane gas explosion ripped through an under-construction tunnel at the state-owned National Hydroelectric Power Corporation's (NHPC) Teesta Stage-VI project in Sikkim on Monday afternoon, killing at least 20 workers and leaving five others unaccounted for deep inside the mountain.

The blast struck the Adit-3 tunnel at Samardung-Jholungy in Namchi district at approximately 3:40 PM local time on July 20, according to district officials. Twenty-seven workers were inside the tunnel at the time; two managed to escape immediately, while 25 were trapped. Six NHPC officials who rushed in to assist the rescue became trapped themselves, according to AP.

"A sudden release/burst of suspected methane gas — trapped or embedded within the rock strata — took place inside the Head Race Tunnel, which was under construction, resulting in the generation of dense smoke and toxic gases."

— NHPC, official statement

By late Tuesday night, rescue teams had recovered 20 bodies from the tunnel, according to Dainik Bhaskar. Five workers remained unaccounted for. Superintendent of Police Sonam Dolma confirmed that the deceased hailed from West Bengal, Uttarakhand, Assam, and Sikkim, with three victims yet to be identified.

Toxic Gas Hampers a Dangerous Rescue

The rescue operation has been one of the most challenging in recent memory. Methane gas, which reduces oxygen levels and poses explosion risks, accumulated across a 1.5-km stretch inside the tunnel. Rescue teams from the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), and local police have been entering in groups of eight, each equipped with oxygen cylinders that last only 40 minutes.

Several rescuers reportedly fainted during the operation due to poor air quality. Fresh air is being pumped into the tunnel through blast-proof blowers and ventilation pipes, while teams are using shotcrete and rock bolting to stabilize the tunnel roof against further collapses. Small loaders and robotic equipment have been deployed to clear debris, according to Dainik Bhaskar.

"Survival chances for the trapped workers were slim, as rescuers had to battle the fumes, making their task difficult."

— Rajiv Roka, Sikkim state disaster management official, to Reuters

A specialized team equipped with gas-proof protective gear was brought from West Bengal to bolster the operation, district officials told Dainik Jagran. The tunnel is being constructed by Patel Engineering Company as part of the larger Teesta Stage-VI Hydroelectric Power Project, which involves two parallel tunnels each stretching roughly 5 km to carry water from the Teesta River to the plant's turbines.

National Response and Political Fallout

Prime Minister Narendra Modi expressed grief over the tragedy and announced an ex-gratia payment of ₹2 lakh from the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund for the next of kin of each deceased worker. Injured workers will receive ₹50,000 in financial assistance. President Droupadi Murmu called the incident "deeply tragic," while Union Home Minister Amit Shah spoke with Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang to review rescue operations and assured central assistance.

Tamang, who visited the blast site, pledged to constitute a high-level enquiry committee. "The State Government will constitute a high-level enquiry committee to ascertain the exact cause of this unfortunate incident," he wrote on Facebook. NHPC also committed to a detailed investigation, stating it was "extending full support to the rescue agencies and the affected families."

A Fragile Region Under Pressure

The disaster strikes a region already scarred by infrastructure-related catastrophe. In October 2023, a glacial lake outburst flood on the Teesta devastated the Teesta Stage-V dam at Chungthang and damaged Stage-VI infrastructure, killing dozens and displacing thousands. NHPC's Teesta-V power station remains non-operational as restoration work continues.

India's push to expand hydropower capacity in the ecologically fragile northeastern Himalayas has drawn persistent criticism from geologists, environmentalists, and local communities who argue that the region's unstable geology — prone to seismic activity, landslides, and gas pockets — makes large-scale tunneling hazardous. The 2023 Uttarkashi tunnel collapse, which trapped 41 workers for 17 days before a dramatic rescue, underscored those risks on a global stage.

The trapped workers — 21 employees of contractor Patel Engineering and six NHPC personnel — represent the migrant labor force that powers India's infrastructure ambitions, often working in remote and dangerous conditions far from home. Rescue operations continued into Wednesday morning as teams pushed toward the five missing workers still inside the mountain.
image_caption: Rescue teams work at the site of the tunnel blast at the NHPC Teesta Stage-VI Hydroelectric Project in Sikkim's Namchi district. Twenty bodies have been recovered from the methane-filled tunnel, with five workers still missing.
nri_angle: The tragedy raises safety questions about India's ambitious hydropower expansion in the Himalayas, a region where diaspora families have roots and where the 2023 Uttarkashi tunnel collapse drew global attention.
